result.rule: Distinguish message tasks from message events: a task models performed work; an event models a message occurrence affecting flow.
Model every distinct activity, event, participant, decision, branch, loop, message and outcome stated in the description. Do not invent process facts.

Do not use a receive label, and do not add detail the description does not attach to the action. Use a receive task or a message event only when the description says the information arrives from another party.

When the description states that the process begins with an action performed by a participant, not with a received message: Model a plain start event whose name does not repeat the described action or its result. Place a task for that action directly after the start event and before the activities that follow it. Do not let the start event itself stand for the action.

When the description says that a follow-up activity or the conclusion of the process happens only after a stated time window or deadline has ended: Model the moment the time window ends as an intermediate catch event placed directly before the follow-up activity or the end event. Do not model the waiting itself as a task, and do not let an activity stand for the passing of time.

When the description says the process ends only after a period of time elapses or a condition becomes true, following earlier activities: Model the waiting for the period to elapse or the condition to become true as an intermediate catch event (timer or conditional) placed before the end event on the sequence path. Do not model the wait as a task, because a task performs work and does not wait for an external time or condition.

result.rule: When the description states, in one sentence, that an actor selects or provides several distinct kinds of information (for example several choices, or personal data together with payment data) after a single verb, and each kind is a separate input the actor supplies: Model each distinct kind of input as its own task, in the order the description states them, connected by sequence flows. Do not combine them into one task whose label lists all the items. Keep each task label to the verb and its single main object, using the description's own words.

When The description states that a participant itself performs an action (for example selecting, providing, or sending something) as a step of the process, rather than the information arriving from another party.: Model that action as a task labeled with the verb the description uses for the participant's action, and keep the label to that verb and its main object. Do not use a receive label, and do not add detail the description does not attach to the action. Use a receive task or a message event only when the description says the information arrives from another party.

When the description joins two distinct actions within one clause with 'and', and presents each action as its own step or outcome: Model each action as a separate task, in the order the description states them, connected by sequence flows. Do not merge them into one task whose label combines the actions. If the clause ends the flow, let the end event represent the final outcome without absorbing the separate task.

When the description states an activity as a verb and object, followed by a purpose, scope or qualifying clause in the same sentence: Name the task with the verb and object of the stated activity, using the description's own words, and leave the purpose or scope clause out of the task label. Do not append words from that clause, and do not add a qualifier the description does not attach to the activity itself.
